prime.problem: When land appears one cell at a time and you need the island count after every addition, rerunning a flood fill each time costs O(k·mn). You need a structure that merges groups and answers "same group?" in near-constant time.
prime.fits: Fifth graph card. It answers incrementally what the flood-fill card answers in one shot, and it becomes Kruskal's cycle test on the minimum spanning tree card.
prime.goal: Implement union–find with both tricks, trace Number of Islands II, and explain why a find costs α(n) ≤ 4 amortized.

attend: What does the root of a tree mean, and why is comparing two roots enough to answer "same island?"
In the island formula, why does the count drop only when a union joins two different roots?
Which trick keeps trees shallow before any find happens, and which one flattens them during finds?
What kind of operation can union–find never support, and what do people do instead?

must: Each group has one root that points at itself → find walks parent pointers to it → two items are connected exactly when their roots match → union only relinks one root
Hang the smaller tree under the bigger root → a node's depth grows only when its group at least doubles → depth ≤ log₂ n (13 for 8,192); add path compression → α(n) ≤ 4 amortized per operation
Without either trick, unions in the wrong order build a chain → finding all 10,000 items costs n(n − 1)/2 = 49,995,000 hops vs 9,999 with the tricks
Unions only merge → no way to split a group → deletions need another approach (process the operations backwards so they become additions)
elevated: Only land cells enter the parent dict → off-grid and water neighbours are simply absent → no bounds checks needed, and space is O(k) not O(m·n)
reference: union by rank (height) as the textbook alternative to size
the exact α(n) bound and CLRS §21.4
the source's stray self and missing colon
path halving as a one-pass variant

compress.prompt: Without scrolling, write find and union (with union by size and path compression) in under 15 lines, then explain in two sentences why islands after an add = islands before + 1 − successful unions.
checklist: find: walk to the root, then repoint the path at it
union: find both roots; if equal return False; else small under big, add sizes
a new land cell starts as its own island (+1)
each union that merges two different roots removes one island
unions between cells already in one island change nothing

retrieve.q: Explain why union by size alone caps the depth at log₂ n.
answer: an item gets one level deeper only when its root goes under a root at least as big
so its group size at least doubles each time
a group can double at most log₂ n times

retrieve.q: Trace step 5 of the card's example, adding (1, 1): which neighbours are unioned in which order, which root wins each time, and what is the island count after?
Island ids per cell, flood fill per add, or union–find: compare them for 10⁴ adds on a 100 × 100 grid, and say when the simplest one is still the right choice.
answer: recount per add: 50,005,000 cell visits in the worst case
island ids: O(1) query but a merge rewrites a whole island
union–find: at most 4 unions per add, α(n) each
for one static grid, a single flood fill is just as fast and simpler

compare.q: Both can count islands. What does union–find remember between queries that flood fill throws away, and what does it lose (compared with flood fill) about the shape of each island?
answer: union–find keeps a forest of roots, so each new cell is merged in α(n)
flood fill recomputes from scratch each time
union–find knows only membership: no paths, no distances, no direction

compare.q: Kruskal asks union–find one question per edge. What is the question, and what would Kruskal cost if that question needed a DFS instead?
answer: are u and v already in the same piece? (would this edge close a cycle?)
with union–find: near O(1) per edge, so sorting dominates
with a DFS per edge: O(V) each, O(E·V) total

predict.q: Feed the positions in the order (2,1), (1,2), (0,0), (0,1), (1,1) instead. Predict the answer list and the final root, before tracing.
predict.answer: [1, 2, 3, 3, 1]. The first three cells are isolated (1, 2, 3), (0,1) joins (0,0) so the count stays 3, and (1,1) merges all three islands (3 + 1 − 3 = 1). The final root is (0,0): at step 5, (1,1)'s up neighbour (0,1) is unioned first, and the {(0,0),(0,1)} group is bigger than each single-cell island, so it absorbs the rest.

apply.task: Use union–find for Redundant Connection: given undirected edges in order, return the first edge whose two ends already share a root. Run it on [[1,2],[1,3],[2,3]] and on [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,4],[1,5]].
apply.done: You return [2, 3] and [1, 4], and you can say why that edge closes a cycle (its ends already had the same root before the union).
apply.hint: Your union already returns False when the roots match; the answer is the first edge for which it does.
